newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya asks IMF for time to meet demands on reform.
newsitem.headline: Kenya asks IMF for time to meet demands on reform.

text.p: Kenya's finance minister said on Thursday the government had asked the International Monetary Fund to extend a deadline for it to fight corruption or lose a big aid package.
"We did ask for extra time and in that context we are waiting for an answer," Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi told a news conference in Nairobi. "I am crossing my fingers."
The IMF deadline had been due to expire on Thursday.
"We are in the middle of consultation. We are still talking with (IMF headquarters in) Washington," said the minister, adding that negotiations on the aid package had not collapsed.
The IMF demanded last month that the government take action to show its commitment to fight corruption and reform the energy sector or it would let the three-year aid package lapse.
The shilling fell against the dollar and pound on Thursday because of market uncertainty ahead of the IMF decision.
Foreign exchange dealers said the Nairobi market was nervous as foreign investors and business managers awaited the IMF verdict, which was expected to be announced in Washington.
The shilling weakened to 58.92 to the U.S. dollar on Thursday, down from Wednesday's 58.06 close.
The IMF extended a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) loan worth $205 million in April last year but payments were conditional on Kenya meeting promises on reform.

The last scheduled ESAF payment, $36 million, was delayed by the IMF for a month from June 30, mainly because of its concern at the way Kenyan authorities had handled the multi-million dollar Goldenberg International financial scandal.
The IMF hit out at the government failure to "take decisive steps to ensure transparency and accountability in the use of public funds and to resolve outstanding energy sector reform".
Mudavadi said on Thursday losing the ESAF would be a blow to Kenya, where President Daniel arap Moi, 73, is seeking re-election this year in the face of opposition demands for political reforms.
"This could have serious repercussions. It could dent investor confidence, affect the shilling, affect inflation and it is something that could shake confidence in the economy," he said.
He said the government was drafting a bill to combat corruption but this was not enough to meet the IMF demands.
"We look forward to legislation. But this in itself is not enough. It must also be supported by action in terms of a process of law that is adhered to and respected," he said.
The IMF has quoted Goldenberg International to illustrate just how Kenyan authorities are reluctant to punish corruption.

In 1991 and 1992 the government paid a company called Goldenberg International about $100 million under an export compensation scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya produces little gold and has no diamond deposits.
Energy Ministry officials also said a bill was being drafted to set up an independent energy regulatory board. Mudavadi has said the bill was one of the items on the IMF's agenda.

Moi's government blunted an opposition-backed rally in the Indian Ocean city of Mombasa at the weekend by licensing it after clashes elsewhere in June and July between police and pro-reform demonstrators rattled foreign investors and tourists. ($1=58.9 Kenyan Shillings)
